rationale: The evidence pack shows Claude Code reading CLAUDE.md project files and integrating with tools like Google Drive/Jira/Slack, but there is no mention of fetching or being pointed at llms.txt or other agent-oriented documentation standards.

Docs explicitly describe CLI composability for CI use ('run it in CI', piping logs), scheduled/automated runs for recurring tasks like overnight CI failure analysis, GitHub PR-triggered code review, and an Agent SDK for building custom automated agents—directly supporting headless/CI automation. No community evidence directly contradicts headless/CI use, though general reliability complaints exist elsewhere.

The evidence pack contains no mention of MCP (Model Context Protocol) or an official MCP server for Claude Code; only general references to custom tooling and an Agent SDK are present, which don't confirm this specific capability.

Claude Code is Anthropic's official command-line agent, run from the terminal, composable with Unix pipes/CI, integrating with git and other tools directly from the CLI. Community evidence confirms it is used and shipped as an interactive CLI (not an editor plugin), corroborating official-CLI delivery despite some quality/trust complaints unrelated to CLI existence.

Claude Code exposes an Agent SDK for building custom agents with control over orchestration, tool access, and permissions, and integrates via CLI, CI, and scripting per docs, but the evidence pack lacks details on a formal REST/HTTP public API contract or comprehensive API reference documentation.

The evidence pack shows Claude Code's general agentic/tooling capabilities and Agent SDK for building custom agents, but contains no mention of scoped or least-privilege API credential issuance/management for agents.

Docs confirm an official Agent SDK exists for building custom agents on top of Claude Code's tools with orchestration and permission control, directly supporting the story, but the evidence pack offers only a single brief mention with no detail on SDK languages, API completeness, or developer experience, and no community validation of SDK usage.

The evidence pack shows scheduling, hooks-like automation (scheduled runs, GitHub integration, Slack routing), and SDK for building custom agents, but no mention of a webhook subscription mechanism allowing external systems to subscribe to Claude Code events.

Docs explicitly describe scheduling ("Run Claude on a schedule... overnight CI failure analysis, weekly dependency audits"), trigger-based automation (Slack mentions, GitHub PR review), and long-running/remote sessions, which directly map to the always-on agent story. However, community reports of unreliable self-verification, degrading output quality, and failure to safely iterate autonomously suggest the autonomous maintenance/fix capability is not fully dependable in practice.

The evidence pack contains no mention of API key authentication as an alternative to account login for Claude Code; docs focus on features/workflows and community items discuss unrelated issues like trust, code quality, and pricing complaints.

Claude Code's docs explicitly state it maps and explains entire codebases via agentic search, understanding project structure and dependencies without manual context selection, directly addressing the story's need to grasp codebase layout before editing. No community evidence specifically disputes this codebase-mapping capability, though most community commentary focuses on implementation reliability rather than comprehension.

Official docs explicitly state Claude Code stages changes, writes commit messages, creates branches, and opens pull requests, and this is reinforced by broader GitHub/GitLab workflow integration claims. No community evidence directly contradicts this specific git-workflow capability.

Claude Code's official docs explicitly advertise a 'GitHub Code Review' feature that provides automatic code review on every PR, and community feedback (comm-18) corroborates that Claude performs well as a reviewer, often needing only one round of fixes. No community evidence specifically disputes the PR review feature, though details on depth of contextual feedback are limited.

Anthropic's docs explicitly claim Claude Code can write tests, fix lint errors, resolve merge conflicts, and update dependencies, closely matching the story. However, community reports raise significant reliability caveats—self-verification failures, degrading output quality, and unreliable automated edits—suggesting these capabilities work but require oversight rather than being fully trustworthy.

No evidence in the pack describes an automatic model-selection or model-routing feature; docs only mention model use indirectly (e.g., Opus draining tokens) but no automatic 'pick best model per task' capability is documented.

Docs describe robust cloud/async capabilities—long-running cloud sessions, teleport, remote control, Slack-to-PR workflows, automatic GitHub code review, and multi-agent orchestration—that align with building, testing, and delivering a reviewable feature end-to-end. However, hands-on community reports describe frequent failures to self-verify, destructive edits (e.g., replace_all bugs), degrading output quality, and near-100% failure rates on some tasks, directly undercutting the reliability implied by the docs.

Docs explicitly describe kicking off long-running tasks in the cloud/web ('work on repos you don't have locally', 'kick off cloud sessions', 'claude --teleport'), matching the story of delegating background work to an isolated cloud environment. No community evidence directly contradicts this specific capability, though overall reliability concerns exist elsewhere.

Anthropic documents the Agent SDK as giving developers 'full control over orchestration, tool access, and permissions,' and Claude Code supports integrations like Jira/Slack/custom tooling that leads could presumably scope. However, community reports describe undisclosed, silently-injected 'fake_tools' definitions and other opaque behaviors baked into every API request, undermining the claim that an engineering lead has full visibility or control over which tools the agent can access.

Docs describe explicit cross-device continuity features: 'Remote Control' to keep working from phone/browser, and `claude --teleport` to pull a task started on web or mobile into the terminal, plus cloud sessions for long-running tasks checked back on later.

Claude Code supports CLAUDE.md, a persistent project file read at the start of every session, giving some cross-session context continuity, but this is a manually authored/maintained file rather than an agent that automatically builds and recalls memory. Community evidence even notes CLAUDE.md files 'exploding' from manual upkeep, indicating no automatic memory formation.

Claude Code supports customization via CLAUDE.md project instructions, integration of custom tooling (Jira, Slack, Drive), and an Agent SDK for building agents with custom tool access/permissions, but the evidence pack shows no dedicated 'skills' marketplace or packaging system explicitly named as such.

Official docs explicitly state the desktop app supports reviewing diffs visually and running multiple sessions side by side, directly matching the story. No community evidence contradicts this specific capability, though it remains vendor-sourced only.

No evidence in the pack mentions SSO, SAML, OIDC, enterprise identity providers, or cloud platform authentication (e.g., AWS/GCP/Azure IAM) for Claude Code; the docs focus on coding workflow features and community evidence discusses reliability/trust issues, not identity/auth integration.

No explicit documentation on the sign-in flow is present, but community evidence (comm-19) mentions using 'a pro plan with Sonnet' with Claude Code, implying subscription-based access exists rather than requiring a separate API key. This is indirect and not confirmed by first-party docs in the evidence pack.

Official docs explicitly state Claude Code can read Google Drive docs, update Jira tickets, and pull data from Slack, plus support custom tooling, directly matching the story. However, this is a single vendor-doc claim with no community evidence or hands-on detail confirming ease of setup or reliability of these integrations.

No evidence in the pack mentions signing in with a personal/Claude.ai account, free-tier access, or avoiding API key management for Claude Code; all docs items describe agentic coding features, not authentication/pricing model.

Vendor docs explicitly state Claude Code 'maps and explains entire codebases in a few seconds' using agentic search 'without you having to manually select context files,' directly matching the story. No community evidence specifically contradicts this codebase-mapping claim, though general reliability concerns exist elsewhere in the evidence.

Evidence describes Claude Code as an agentic CLI/task-based tool that plans, writes, and verifies code across files, integrates with git/CI, and has IDE plugins with diff viewing—but nothing indicates inline, as-you-type code completions or next-edit suggestions like a traditional autocomplete tool.

Docs explicitly claim Claude Code reads issues, writes code, runs tests, and submits PRs end-to-end (docs-16, docs-3, docs-11), suggesting full issue-to-PR automation. However, community reports describe significant reliability problems—self-verification failures, careless replace-all bugs, and even a user reporting a '100% failure rate' over a month—casting doubt on how reliably this end-to-end flow actually works in practice.

Official docs explicitly describe a JetBrains plugin (IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, etc.) offering interactive diff viewing and selection context sharing, directly matching the story. No community evidence contradicts this specific IDE integration claim, though corroboration is limited to vendor docs.

No evidence anywhere in the pack indicates Claude Code surfaces license attribution or public-code matching references for suggested code; docs focus on coding, git workflow, review automation, and integrations without any mention of code provenance/license scanning.

Documentation shows a page titled 'Debug live web applications | Chrome', indicating the capability exists, but the evidence gives no scope or mechanism detail; calibrated to partial to match the evidentiary bar applied to competing products. (Downgraded from full following an adversarial bias audit — the judge model and this product share a vendor.)

Claude Code is explicitly designed and documented as a terminal-native coding agent that plans, writes, tests, and commits code locally, with community evidence confirming it runs as a CLI/bash tool rather than an editor plugin.

The evidence pack describes codebase mapping, multi-agent parallelism, and remote/cloud sessions, but none of the provided items mention adding or referencing multiple project directories within a single session for combined context.

Claude Code offers a JetBrains IDE plugin with interactive diff viewing and context sharing (claude-code-docs-19), implying some in-IDE integration, but its core interface is a terminal/CLI tool rather than a native chat panel, and community feedback explicitly criticizes it for being 'shipped as an interactive CLI instead of an extension' compared to IDE-native competitors.

The evidence pack contains no mention of selecting between multiple AI model providers within Claude Code; all documentation references only Claude Code's own agentic and workflow features tied to Anthropic's Claude models.

Docs show direct Slack integration (@Claude mention triggers PR) and GitHub/GitLab integration for reading issues and submitting PRs, plus GitHub Code Review on PRs, but there's no evidence of native Linear integration or a general 'kick off from any of these platforms' unified experience—GitLab support is limited to CLI workflow, not agent-triggering from GitLab UI itself.

The evidence pack describes Claude Code as a CLI/terminal-based coding agent that works from plain-language instructions, git, docs, and integrations, but contains no mention of accepting image, sketch, or PDF design inputs to generate an app.

Docs explicitly support natural-language debugging (live web app debugging via Chrome, CI failure analysis, codebase mapping/explanation, lint fixing) and Claude Code is described as understanding and querying entire codebases conversationally. However, community reports raise significant reliability caveats—self-verification failures, unreliable 'fixes', and degraded troubleshooting performance—tempering the polished vendor claims.

Docs explicitly claim the core workflow (describe in plain language → Claude plans, writes code across multiple files, verifies it works), but community reports include serious reliability complaints such as unsafe replace_all corrupting code, 'simplest fix' producing broken output, and a user reporting a 100% failure rate on real tasks, alongside others praising its coding strength.

Docs explicitly describe spawning multiple parallel sub-agents coordinated by a lead agent, running multiple sessions/cloud tasks in parallel, and kicking off long-running or scheduled tasks that can be checked on later or run overnight — directly supporting fleets of parallel, long-running agents. However, no evidence confirms sustained multi-day autonomy in practice, and community reports raise reliability concerns (self-verification failures, degrading output quality over long sessions) that caveat claims of dependable hours/days-long unattended operation.

Docs describe running multiple sessions/tasks in parallel and reviewing diffs visually, which supports parallel task attempts and comparison, but there's no explicit workflow for spawning multiple attempts of the same task and selecting the best one—only community evidence is unrelated to this specific capability.

Claude Code supports custom tooling integrations (Jira, Slack, Drive, GitHub/GitLab) and an Agent SDK to build custom agents on its tool platform, suggesting some ecosystem extensibility, but there is no explicit evidence of a marketplace or mechanism for integrating other partners' pre-built agent apps into workflows.

Claude Code explicitly supports a CLAUDE.md file placed at the project root that is read at the start of every session, serving exactly as a persistent instructions file for standards/conventions, and community evidence confirms developers actively use and expand these files in practice.

Docs confirm Claude Code supports visual diff review, automatic PR code review, running tests, and IDE diff viewing (docs-12,13,16,19), directly enabling pre-merge inspection and checks. However, community reports raise concerns about self-verification reliability (e.g., unnoticed replace_all bugs) suggesting the tool's own 'verifies it works' claims aren't fully trustworthy, so human diff review remains essential.

The evidence describes cloud/background sessions and CLAUDE.md for instructions, but nothing about defining a reproducible environment (e.g., dependency setup, install scripts, devcontainer config) for cloud sessions to run repos with required tooling.

Docs claim Claude Code maps codebases for root-cause analysis, debugs live apps via Chrome, runs tests, and 'verifies it works' as part of its workflow (docs-2, docs-15, docs-17, docs-8, docs-16). However, community reports directly contradict the self-verification claim, describing unreliable fixes (e.g., replace_all corrupting constants) and stating 'You absolutely can't trust it to self-verify,' with one user reporting a 100% failure rate over a month.

The evidence pack describes Claude Code's coding, git, integration, and automation features but contains no mention of sandboxed execution, restricted network access, or containerized tool/network isolation for safety review purposes.

Claude Code offers CLAUDE.md as a shared, versionable context file read at every session and can pull in docs from Google Drive, Jira, and Slack, which could serve as building blocks for a shared source of truth. However, there is no evidence of a dedicated 'workspace' construct for aggregating docs and repos as a persistent team knowledge base—these are ad hoc integrations rather than a purpose-built shared workspace feature.

Docs explicitly describe non-interactive/automation usage: piping logs, running in CI, chaining with other tools per Unix philosophy, scheduled runs for recurring automation, and SDK for building custom orchestrations — all directly supporting scripted non-interactive workflows.
The evidence pack contains no documentation or community discussion of a data/training opt-out policy or setting for Claude Code; only unrelated features and trust/security complaints are present.

Docs describe a unified workspace for running multiple sessions side by side, spawning parallel sub-agents coordinated by a lead agent, and kicking off cloud/background tasks (claude-code-docs-6, -13, -14), directly matching the story's intent. However, this is entirely vendor-sourced with no independent community validation of the multi-session management UX, and general community feedback raises reliability/trust concerns about Claude Code's agentic behavior that could affect confidence in managing many concurrent sessions.

Claude Code offers general automatic code review on PRs and can explain/map codebases, which could surface issues including vulnerabilities, but the evidence pack contains no explicit mention of dedicated security-vulnerability detection, contextual security explanations, or automated security fixes.

No evidence in the pack mentions llms.txt support, agent-oriented documentation formats, or any mechanism for pointing an agent at machine-readable docs; the pack only covers general agentic coding capabilities and community feedback on model performance.

Codex offers a CLI and API-key access that could support headless/automation use, and cloud tasks can run in parallel without a local machine, but the evidence pack lacks explicit mention of CI integration, non-interactive/exec flags, or scripting support—key elements for a true 'headless in CI' story.

The evidence pack describes Codex's cloud/CLI agent capabilities, integrations with GitHub, GitLab, Linear, and Slack, and various community reactions, but contains no mention of an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server or MCP connectivity for Codex.

Codex CLI is officially documented as OpenAI's local coding agent (codex-gh-1), with sign-in via ChatGPT plans or API key (codex-gh-3, codex-gh-4), and is referenced as a core workflow interface alongside the web app (codex-docs-7). Community discussion also treats Codex CLI as a real, actively used tool, confirming it functions in practice despite performance complaints unrelated to its existence as a CLI.

GitHub docs mention Codex can be used with an API key (though requiring extra setup), suggesting some programmatic access exists, but there's no dedicated public API documentation and community evidence explicitly states the current flagship model 'isn't available on the API yet' pending safety review, contradicting a fully documented, ready-to-use public API.

Evidence shows Codex can be used with an API key requiring 'additional setup' (codex-gh-4), but there is no mention of scoped, least-privilege, or granular API credential/permission controls for agents anywhere in the pack; in fact community comments raise concerns about sandboxing and unrestricted file system access (codex-comm-7, codex-comm-10).

Evidence shows Codex can be used with an API key but 'requires additional setup' and the newer model (gpt-5.3-codex) 'isn't available on the API yet' — there is no mention of official SDKs (Python/Node/etc.) for building agentic integrations, only CLI/IDE/chat plan usage.

No evidence in the pack mentions webhooks or event subscription capabilities for Codex; the documentation focuses on task delegation, cloud environments, and integrations with GitHub/Slack/Linear as triggers, not outbound webhook subscriptions.

Codex supports task delegation from triggers like GitHub PRs/issues, Linear, and Slack, and can run tasks in parallel cloud environments, but there is no explicit evidence of scheduled/cron-based always-on agents that autonomously maintain software over time.

GitHub docs confirm API key authentication is possible as an alternative to ChatGPT account login, but explicitly note it 'requires additional setup' and the default recommended path is account-based login. Community evidence also suggests newer models aren't yet available via API, undercutting full parity.

The evidence pack covers Codex's task delegation, cloud execution, model performance, and UX complaints, but contains no evidence of features for exploring, summarizing, or navigating a codebase's architecture to help a developer find where to start making changes.

Docs confirm Codex can start work from GitHub PRs/issues, inspect diffs, and open pull requests when done, and it integrates with GitHub as a native workflow entry point, covering staging, commits, branches, and PR creation as an agent-driven flow.

Evidence shows Codex can be triggered from GitHub PRs/issues to perform coding tasks and produce diffs, but there is no evidence of an automatic code-review feature that posts contextual feedback on every pull request.

Codex is documented as a general delegate-a-task coding agent that edits files, produces diffs, and opens PRs (codex-docs-5,6), which implicitly covers tasks like tests, lint fixes, or dependency bumps, but no evidence explicitly confirms merge-conflict resolution or dependency updates. Community feedback is mixed—some praise it as reliable for editing/testing workflows (codex-comm-8) while others say it 'struggles with almost anything' (codex-comm-3), so real-world reliability for these specific tasks is uncertain.

No evidence in the pack describes Codex automatically selecting the best model per task; users manually choose models (e.g., gpt-5.3-codex, gpt-5.3-codex-spark) and community comments discuss switching between models/providers manually, not automatic model selection.

OpenAI's docs describe a cloud agent that runs tasks in isolated environments, produces diffs/summaries, and opens PRs for review—matching the build/test/demo-for-review workflow (codex-docs-1,5,6). But community hands-on reports are split: some call it 'shockingly good' and comparable to a junior engineer (codex-comm-18), while others report it 'struggles with almost anything,' lacks real agentic competence versus competitors, and hits tight usage limits that interrupt end-to-end workflows (codex-comm-3, codex-comm-13, codex-comm-8).

Codex docs explicitly describe delegating tasks to run in isolated cloud environments in parallel, starting from web/GitHub/GitLab/Linear/Slack, and returning later to review diffs or open PRs — a direct match to the story. Community evidence discusses model performance/UX issues but doesn't dispute the cloud-delegation capability itself.

Evidence shows Codex integrates with GitHub, GitLab, Linear, and Slack and lets you configure per-repo tooling/setup, but there is no evidence of an engineering-lead-level permission system to selectively allow/deny which external tools or integrations the agent can access. Community comments even raise concerns about lack of sandboxing/control over file system and app access, but no counter-evidence of an actual admin control feature exists.

Codex cloud tasks can be started from web, GitHub, GitLab, Linear, or Slack and later reviewed or continued from the web or CLI, enabling cross-device task continuity, as described in multiple docs entries.

The evidence pack contains no mention of persistent memory, cross-session recall, or automatic memory-building features for Codex; documentation focuses on task delegation, parallel cloud runs, and repo setup, not memory persistence.

The evidence pack describes Codex's environment setup, cloud task execution, IDE/CLI integration, and community commentary on model performance/UX, but contains no mention of a skills system, plugin/extension marketplace, or mechanism for equipping the agent with custom specialized skills.

Docs confirm diff review ('inspect the summary and diff') and parallel task execution across cloud sessions, and community posts confirm a native macOS desktop app exists, but there's no direct evidence of a unified UI showing multiple sessions side by side, and the app has reported reliability/platform gaps (Mac-only, loading issues).

Codex supports signing in via a ChatGPT Enterprise plan (codex-gh-3), implying some enterprise account integration, but there is no evidence of SSO/SAML, Okta/Azure AD, or cloud IAM integration for compliance-grade authentication.

GitHub docs explicitly recommend signing in with a ChatGPT account to use Codex under Plus, Pro, Business, Edu, or Enterprise subscription plans, with API key as an alternative requiring extra setup, directly matching the story.

Codex documents integrations with GitHub, GitLab, Linear, and Slack to start tasks and provide context, matching the Slack part of the story, but there is no evidence of Jira or Google Drive connectivity, which are explicitly named in the story.

Codex CLI documentation confirms signing in with a ChatGPT account (Plus/Pro/Business/Edu/Enterprise) avoids needing to manage API keys, and API key use requires 'additional setup'. However, no evidence indicates a genuinely free tier—only paid ChatGPT plan-based access—and community comments describe tight usage quotas/limits under this login model.

Codex is described as an autonomous coding agent that operates on the whole repo without needing manual file selection (codex-gh-1, codex-docs-4/6), implying it can explore and explain code, but no evidence explicitly confirms a 'map and explain unfamiliar codebase' feature, and community feedback highlights inconsistent competence on complex tasks (codex-comm-3, codex-comm-13).

Codex is positioned as an agentic coding assistant that delegates tasks, works in cloud sandboxes, or runs via CLI/IDE extension to make larger edits — none of the evidence describes inline, IDE-native autocomplete-style code completions or next-edit suggestions as the user types. All docs and community discussion focus on task delegation, diffs, PRs, and agent behavior, not real-time inline completions.

Docs explicitly describe starting tasks from GitHub issues/PRs, running them in isolated cloud environments, inspecting the diff, and opening a pull request when ready—directly matching the end-to-end issue-to-PR workflow. Evidence confirms Codex integrates with VS Code, Cursor, and Windsurf editors, but no mention of JetBrains IDE support anywhere in the pack, nor of interactive diff viewing or context-sharing UI within any IDE.
